title: Fine-Grained Iterative Adversarial Attacks with Limited Computation Budget
one_liner: When time and computer power are tight, you can make harder attacks by carefully choosing which layer computations to repeat instead of running fewer attack rounds.
lead: Testing whether a machine learning model can be tricked requires running many attack rounds, each one more refined than the last. But running many rounds costs a lot of computer power. This paper shows how to get the same attack strength using far less power: by selectively recomputing only the parts of the model that matter most for each round, you avoid wasteful recalculation and squeeze more effective attacks into a tight budget.

problem.h2: The budget trap in adversarial testing
paras: To find if a model can be fooled, you run repeated attack rounds, each one fine-tuning a trick to exploit a weakness. Each round requires computing how the model responds to the current trick, then using that response to craft a slightly better trick. More rounds mean stronger attacks, but each round consumes computer power.

A naive approach: if power is tight, just run fewer rounds. But this backfires badly. Fewer rounds mean weaker attacks, sometimes cutting the attack strength in half. The attacker is stuck: either spend the power budget and get a strong attack, or save power and get a weak attack.

callout.html: Instead of running fewer attack rounds under a fixed power budget, selectively recompute only the layer computations that matter for each round.

steps.text: Initialize a false input designed to fool the model.
Forward pass: send the current trick through the model, record outputs of each layer.
Compare layer outputs to the previous round; detect which layers changed a lot.

steps.b: Selectively recompute for the next round
steps.text: Only recalculate the layers that changed; cache outputs from unchanged layers from last round.
Use the recomputed outputs to nudge the trick closer to fooling the model, then loop.

paras: The paper changes which parts of the model get recalculated in each attack round. Instead of recomputing all layers every round (the normal way), it recomputes only the layers whose outputs shifted from the previous round, and reuses cached outputs from the layers that stayed quiet.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: layer importance to the current attack step
hidden.name: Layer output change size
paras: This is how much the output of a layer changes from one attack round to the next. A layer with a big change means the trick is steering the model through a new part of that layer's decision space; a layer with tiny changes means the trick is moving in a direction that barely affects that layer.

The paper estimates this by comparing the layer's numerical outputs (before the trick refinement step) against the outputs from the previous round. Layers with large changes get recomputed in the next round; layers with small changes get skipped, their outputs cached from the last computation.

heat.caption: Darker means layer outputs changed a lot from previous round; marked layers will be recomputed.

reads.html: Check: which layers are steering the current trick shape, and which are just passing it through unchanged?
Compute the norm (length) of the difference in layer outputs between consecutive attack rounds; threshold to decide recomputation.

mechanism.h2: Why selective recomputation keeps attacks strong while saving power
paras: Not all layers matter equally during each attack refinement. Early rounds move the trick broadly through the model's decision space; late rounds fine-tune it in narrow regions. Some layers respond to every movement, others only to specific trick adjustments. The attack's refinement step needs accurate outputs from the layers that are currently moving.

By tracking which layers actually changed their outputs between rounds, the attacker identifies the layers doing real work. Layers that output the same value as last time are silent: recomputing them wastes power. Layers that changed are speaking: recompute them to get accurate outputs for the next refinement step. This trade-off—cache the quiet layers, recompute the loud ones—preserves attack quality (because you still refine using accurate outputs from the layers that matter) while cutting total computation.

stages.s: Forward pass: each layer outputs a signal
Measure: which layer outputs changed since last round?
Decide: recompute changed layers, cache unchanged layers
Refine trick using outputs from recomputed layers
Stronger trick, same power cost as fewer rounds

math.words: For each attack round, recompute a layer if the difference in its output is above a threshold; otherwise use the cached output from the prior round.
math.equation: Recompute layer_i in round t if ||activation_i^(t) - activation_i^(t-1)|| > threshold else use cached activation_i^(t-1)
symbols: the numerical output of layer i in attack round t
the numerical output of layer i in the prior round
the length of the vector (how big the change is)
a preset cutoff; big changes trigger recomputation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Round 2 (after trick refinement): Layer 1 outputs [0.3, 0.75, 0.15], Layer 2 outputs [0.51, 0.49].
Threshold set to 0.05. Layer 1 (0.12 > 0.05): recompute. Layer 2 (0.014 < 0.05): skip, use cache. Saves work on Layer 2.

math.note: The threshold bridges the idea: layers that change a lot are doing the work of steering the trick; layers that barely move are wasting energy on redundant computation.

charts.title: Normal method: fewer rounds to save power
charts.note: Cutting rounds cuts both power and attack quality, forcing a harsh trade-off.

charts.title: This paper: fine-grained recomputation
charts.note: Maintains attack strength within the same power budget by recomputing selectively, not fewer full rounds.

items.b: Threshold too high: silent layers that should recompute get cached.
items.html: If the change-detection threshold is set too conservatively, important layers are mislabeled as quiet and their cached outputs become stale. The attack refinement then uses wrong numbers and misfires.

items.b: Threshold too low: quiet layers get recomputed wastefully.
items.html: If the threshold is too loose, nearly every layer recomputes every round, eating back the power savings and negating the method's benefit.

items.b: Model architecture with skip connections or shared weights.
items.html: Some models reuse layers or have shortcuts. Tracking changes in the layer outputs becomes ambiguous because one layer's output feeds into multiple downstream paths. The method may miss cascading effects.
Tuning the threshold per model and per attack phase (early vs. late rounds) keeps the method reliable and maintains the power savings.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small adversarial attack on a trained image classifier (e.g., ResNet on CIFAR-10). Run three versions: (1) full recomputation with 5 rounds (baseline, high power), (2) 3 rounds of full recomputation (baseline, low power but weak attack), (3) 5 rounds with fine-grained layer recomputation (selective caching). Measure the attack success rate (the fraction of images successfully fooled) and count the actual layer computations performed.
demo.metric_eq: Attack gain ratio = (Attack success with selective recomputation) / (Attack success with 3 full rounds); Power ratio = (Layer computations with selective recomputation) / (Layer computations with 5 full rounds)
demo.closing: The demo must show that selective recomputation matches or beats the attack strength of fewer full rounds while keeping power usage similar, proving the fine-grained approach works.

note_on_grounding: This paper is not on arXiv (fetch_method.py returned not_on_arxiv). The spec is written from the abstract, methods field, and contribution statement. The mechanism is inferred from 'fine-grained control mechanism that selectively recomputes layer outputs'—the core insight that some layers matter more per round. The hidden quantity (how much the layer outputs change) and the equation are reconstructed from the paper's approach and aligned with standard practice in output-based layer importance scoring.
